The Rolls-Royce share price is slipping… should I buy the stock now?

Even as Rolls-Royce continues to execute its extraordinary turnaround, the share price is starting to experience turbulence. What’s happening?

Posted by
Zaven Boyrazian, CFA ❯
@ZBoyrazian
Zaven is an equity investment analyst. Specialising in corporate valuation, he employs a modern take on the principles set out by Benjamin Graham to identify hidden value in companies that are making the world a better place. Zaven has previously worked in the aerospace and video game industries, holding a Bachelor's degree in Aerospace Engineering, a Master's degree in Investment Management, and has passed the Level 3 CFA exam. “We never can be sure of an outcome, but I think we can get the odds on our side by understanding where we are in the cycle.” - Howard Marks
Published 5 October, 8:01 am BST
| More on: RR.

The Rolls-Royce (LSE:RR.) share price has delivered spectacular returns in recent years, transforming the company into one of the highest-performing stocks in the entire FTSE 100 since 2021.

But lately, that explosive momentum has started fading. Since reaching 1,586p in early August, the shares have drifted almost 8% lower to around 1,462p today. Is this a sign that the momentum is fading? Or is it just a temporary pause in a much longer bull run?

Should you buy Rolls-Royce Plc shares today?

Before you decide, please take a moment to review this report first. Despite ongoing uncertainties from US tariffs to global conflicts, Mark Rogers and his team believe many UK shares still trade at substantial discounts, offering savvy investors plenty of potential opportunities to learn about.

That’s why this could be an ideal time to secure this valuable research – Mark’s analysts have scoured the markets to reveal 5 of his favourite long-term ‘Buys’. Please, don’t make any big decisions before seeing them.

Claim Your Free Copy Now

Why is momentum stalling?

There are a lot of factors at play here. But the recent weakness is certainly not a result of underwhelming financial results. In fact, across the first half of 2026 the engineering group’s underlying revenues surged yet another 26% to £11.3bn alongside an even more impressive 46% bump in operating profits.

Instead, investors are seemingly growing nervous about the valuation. After such an explosive rally, the stock’s earnings multiple jumped to pretty premium levels. And even today after a near-double-digit pullback, Rolls-Royce shares are still trading for just over 40 times its earnings.

Investors have already priced in significant expectations of future growth. So, if any unwanted surprises pop up, it could trigger significant volatility for shareholders.

Is that likely?

It’s impossible to say what’s going to happen over the coming quarters with any real degree of accuracy. However, while full-year financial guidance remains unchanged, large-engine flying hours might be on track to fall towards the lower end of expectations.

Why? Because with oil & gas prices rising sharply, the cost of jet fuel has jumped, leading to a substantial increase in airfares. And in turn, travel demand is likely to take a hit.

With that in mind, it’s not surprising to see some investors start to take some profit. But is this an opportunity for long-term focused investors?

Still firing strongly

While there are some short-term headwinds on the horizon, the long-term outlook remains pretty exciting. Rolls-Royce’s transformation continues to deliver ever-better results with free cash flow in the first half reaching almost £2bn.

As such, the firm’s net cash position is on the rise, giving even more financial flexibility for management to continue paying down its historically troublesome debts in the quest to repair the balance sheet.

The growth in cash flow isn’t coming from just one division either. Civil Aerospace, Defence, and Power Systems all expanded operating profits by 31%, 57%, and 72%, respectively.

Power Systems is benefiting from booming data-centre demand, while the Defence segment is now carrying a £17.5bn order backlog. And while Civil Aerospace might be hitting some turbulence, the division is nonetheless still enjoying a steady stream of shop visits and aftermarket service demand.

So, what’s the verdict?

With the average consensus from institutional analysts sitting near 1,690p per share, the experts seem to think the recent sell-off is unjustified. And if Rolls-Royce’s business operated in a vacuum, I would agree.

However, with external macroeconomic forces applying pressure, issues like supply-chain disruptions and weaker air travel could put some strain on margins, at least in the near term. And while it’s ultimately the long-term that counts, for a stock trading at a premium valuation, ignoring these short-term headwinds could catch many investors off guard.

That’s why I’m not rushing to buy today. Instead, I’ve got my eye on another top-notch FTSE 100 stock…

Should you invest £5,000 in Rolls-Royce Plc right now?

When investing expert Mark Rogers and his team have a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, the flagship Twelfth Magpie Share Advisor newsletter he has run for nearly a decade has provided thousands of paying members with top stock recommendations from the UK and US markets.
